title: Arjuna's mind like the wind
hook: Arjuna says the mind is like the wind, and Krishna gives the same two words as Patanjali
carry: abhyasa and vairagya: practice, and let go
tomorrow: how does a five-year-old become the star that never moves?

segments.voice: Yesterday, nidra, sleep, one of the five turnings, and Indra learning that even in deep sleep, the self is there.
screen: `EVEN IN DEEP SLEEP, THE SELF IS THERE.`

segments.voice: My mind is restless. Holding it still is like holding the wind. That's Arjuna in the Gita, more or less, a few months ago on this path, stopping Krishna somewhere in the sixth chapter. Anyone who has tried to meditate for five minutes knows the feeling. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees: yes, the mind is hard to hold. Then he gives two words for how it's done. Patanjali, in thread twelve, gives the very same two.
screen: `ARJUNA: MY MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Thread twelve: abhyasa vairagyabhyam tan nirodhah. By practice and non-attachment, they are stilled; they, meaning the turnings. Two words carry the whole method. Abhyasa, practice: coming back, again and again, to the thing you've chosen. Vairagya, non-attachment: letting go of the pull. Literally it means without coloring, without the red flower staining the crystal. Teachers often say the two are like the two wings of a bird. One wing alone, and you fly in circles. Practice without letting go becomes grinding: you sit every day, jaw clenched, demanding results. Letting go without practice becomes drifting: you're very relaxed and nothing changes. Coming back, and not clutching. And here is the Gita's answer to Arjuna, in that sixth chapter: the mind is restless, hard to hold, but it can be held by practice and by dispassion. The same pair, in the same order. Two great texts, from different schools, agree on the method. Now make it small, the way Hindus do it. Practice is the next bead on a mala, the name said again each time the mind runs off. Letting go is not needing that sitting to feel special, and not keeping score. Tomorrow and the day after, Patanjali takes each wing on its own.
screen: `ABHYĀSA-VAIRĀGYĀBHYĀṀ TAN-NIRODHAḤ.` · `ABHYASA: COMING BACK, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `VAIRAGYA: LETTING GO OF THE PULL.` · `TWO WINGS OF ONE BIRD.` · then, large: `PRACTICE, AND LET GO.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing to return to: if you pray, a name of God, Rama, Krishna, or Om; if you don't, the breath at the nose. When the mind wanders, and it will, come back without scolding it, no clutching, no scorekeeping: come back, let go, the whole method in small.
Abhyasa vairagya, practice and non-attachment, the turnings are stilled. Two wings: one alone, you fly in circles.
Your line: abhyasa and vairagya, practice, and let go. Krishna told Arjuna the same. One more day to three hundred.

screen: `DAY 299 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE STAR THAT NEVER MOVES.`

howItsDone: Hindu teachers of meditation often pair abhyasa and vairagya, citing both Yoga Sutra 1.12 and Bhagavad Gita 6.35, and describe daily practice as returning again and again without clinging to results.
